To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cattle occupied a prominent place in the economy of the Cistercians of England and Wales and that they were raised on the estates of all the houses, with the possible exception of the small house of Cleeve in the west country.
the Cistercians were not the only monastic Order in England to raise cattle, that their interest in cattle did not begin in I237, and that the prohibition of I237 was not a complete ban.
the Cistercians were not hide traders, that the Cistericans were cattle breeders and that the Cisterican monasteries were not the only places where the monks were cattle breeders.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Cistercians of England and Wales, like other monastic and secular lords, had cattle in their herds, and that they had them in greater numbers than the average of their contemporaries.

cattle, sheep and swine were of roughly equal importance in the economic life of the Order in England and Wales, and that, while the Cistercian interest in sheep and wool was not inconsiderable, it was not paramount.
, although cattle were not always the most important farm animals, they were always important and sometimes very important.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although the Cistercians were not in the forefront of the hide trade, they nevertheless played their part and were not averse to the use of hides and tanning in the management of their estates.
, as far as can be judged, the Cistercians were not primarily a cattle-breeding order, but that they did breed cattle and, when they did, it was usually on a fairly substantial scale.

the Order, in its first century and a half, was not particularly concerned with cattle, and that thereafter it was interested in them, but that the extent of its interest varied greatly from place to place and from time to time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the case of the Cistercian monasteries of England and Wales at least, it is not the case that sheep were always and everywhere second to none among their livestock.
, as the Cistercians' economic activities expanded in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, so the number of cattle they owned and grazed increased and the range of their operations widened.
